land.text: the Tibetan plateau and the Hexi Corridor, held by the rival Tibetan lords after Langdarma's death, without the Dzungaria and Turfan land the Uyghurs had taken in 790-792

successors.note: Cliopatria ends the empire in 849 and starts 'Tibetans' in 850; the dossiers move the break to 842 (Langdarma's assassination) and the new state takes the empire's 842-849 shape. Shazhou and Guazhou fall in 848, Ganzhou, Suzhou and Yizhou by 850 (see tibetans).

capitals.name: Lhasa
capitals.note: Infobox capital: Lhasa. 'The capital was moved in the 7th century from the Yungbulakang Palace to Lhasa' (Tibetan Empire page); the Songtsen Gampo page says only that he moved the seat from the Yarlung Valley to the Kyichu Valley, with no year, so Lhasa is drawn for the whole life.

rulers.name: Songtsen Gampo
rulers.note: List page: 614-648, clipped to the founding year 618; the Tibetan Empire infobox has 618-650 and the Songtsen Gampo page says the Tibetan Annals date his death to 649, with a Tang envoy arriving in 650.

rulers.name: Songtsen Gampo
rulers.note: Second span as the list page prints it ('655-660'); the page does not explain the overlap with Gungsong Gungtsen.

rulers.name: Tride Tsuktsen Me Agtsom
rulers.note: The Tang-Tibet relations page has 'Two ministers killed king Me Agtsom' in 754 and Trisong Detsen taking power in 755; the Tibetan Empire infobox gives Trisong Detsen 753-797.

rulers.name: Ralpachen
rulers.note: Called Tritsuk Detsen in the infobox; murdered in 838 by his brother Langdarma. The list gives no ruler for 838-841.

rulers.name: Langdarma
rulers.note: Assassinated in 842 (Tibetan Empire page); the Tang-Tibet relations page has 846 for his death and 841 for Trisong Detsen's.

correction.text: the Yarlung valley and Lhasa core of Cliopatria's first shape, unchanged

198,000 km2, the Yarlung-Lhasa core; the pages name no frontier for the early 7th century (Namri Songtsen 'besieged the Kingdom of Sumpa in the early 7th century and eventually conquered it'). Stands.

753,000 km2: the step from 623 is the Sumpa conquest, 'defeated the Sumpa in northeastern Tibet circa 627' (Songtsen Gampo page; the Tibetan Empire page has 'Myang Mangpoje defeated the Sumpa people (c. 627)'). Stands.

1.86 M km2, west to 78.0 E: the Zhangzhung step. No change from 638 (1.89 M km2). Princess Wencheng 'left China in 640 ... arriving the next year' (641) and the Tibetans 'reestablished [the Nepalese king] on his throne [in 641]'; Nepal is an ally or client on the page, not territory, and is not drawn. Infobox area 4.6 M km2 is for c. 800 (ratio 0.41 for this shape, not comparable).
1.90 M km2; a small southern step (to 27.35 N) where Kamarupa's seed shows a 656 loss. The Tibetan Empire page is silent on it. Stands, unverified.
1.90 M km2, unchanged. The Tuyuhun conquest follows in the 666 shape ('defeated by the Tibetan army', 663).

region.text: the Yarlung valley and Lhasa core, 198,000 km2

ledger.note: 618: Songtsen Gampo succeeds the assassinated Namri Songtsen and the Tibetan Empire begins. Infobox 'Established: 618'; he was enthroned as a minor 'after his father was poisoned circa 618' (Songtsen Gampo page). No frontier is given for 618; the core is Cliopatria's 623 shape.

region.text: the Sumpa of northeastern Tibet, c. 627

ledger.note: 627: the Sumpa fall. Minister Nyang Mangpoje 'defeated the Sumpa in northeastern Tibet circa 627' (the Tibetan Empire page: 'Myang Mangpoje defeated the Sumpa people (c. 627)'). Region: the step between Cliopatria's 623 and 627 shapes.

region.text: the north and north-east of the plateau added by Cliopatria's 628 shape

ledger.note: 628: the plateau widens north and east. Page silent: Cliopatria's 628 step of 527,000 km2 has no dated sentence on the Tibetan Empire page (the nearest is the 634 submission of 'Zhangzhung and various Qiang tribes'); the stateless tribes of the north-east plateau are the reading.

region.text: Zhangzhung (western Tibet, Ngari) and various Qiang tribes

ledger.note: 634: Zhangzhung submits. 'In 634, Zhangzhung and various Qiang tribes' submitted (Tang Annals, Tibetan Empire page); the Ladakh page has 'Zhangzhung fell victim to Tibet's ambitions in c. 634 and disappeared', while Stein's date is 645 ('In 645, Songtsen Gampo overran the kingdom of Zhangzhung').

region.text: the north-eastern edge of the plateau toward Songzhou

ledger.note: 638: the north-eastern edge moves toward Songzhou. Page silent on ground held: the Songtsen Gampo page has only that Tibet 'attacked Tang affiliates in 637 and 638' and the frontier city of Songzhou; the 37,000 km2 step is Cliopatria's. [Reviewer ea-04-b: counterpart set to tuyuhun, mirroring tuyuhun's 638 loss; the Tuyuhun page has the Tibetan attack after 635-636 and 'The Tuyuhun Empire lost much of its territory in southern Gansu to Tibetans' (no year).]

region.text: the southern edge of the plateau toward Kamarupa, added by Cliopatria's 656 shape

ledger.note: 656: the southern Himalayan edge moves. Page silent; Cliopatria's 656 step (to 27.35 N) is the mirror of the loss in kamarupa-kingdom's seed (Kamarupa is a neighbour 623-655).

region.text: the Tuyuhun ('Azha) lands around Lake Koko Nor

ledger.note: 663: the Tuyuhun fall. The Azha or Tuyuhun kingdom 'was defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture'; the Tang-Tibet relations page has 'In 669 AD, the Tibetans invaded and conquered Tuyuhun kingdom of Qinghai' and the tuyuhun dossier keeps 663. Cliopatria's shape takes the land in 666.

region.text: Khotan and the southern rim of the Tarim Basin

ledger.note: 666: Khotan and the southern Tarim rim. 'Between 665 and 670, Khotan was defeated by the Tibetans' (Tibetan Empire page); the Protectorate page has Yutian attacked in 663 and 665 and conquered only in 792, so the date is disputed. [Reviewer ea-04-b: counterpart was kingdom-of-khotan, whose dossier begins in 851; the earlier Yutian kingdom has no dossier.]

region.text: the Four Garrisons of Anxi (Qiuci, Shule, Yutian, Yanqi) and the Tarim north of the southern rim

ledger.note: 670: the Four Garrisons fall. After winning the Battle of Dafeichuan the Tibetans 'gained control over all of the Chinese Four Garrisons of Anxi in the Tarim Basin in 670'. [Reviewer ea-04-b, 2026-10-19: region trimmed to the Tarim Basin; the Protectorate page has Tibet capture Qiuci and attack Gumo in 670 and reports no Tibetan capture of Xizhou (Turfan) or Tingzhou/Beiting before 790, so Dzungaria and Turfan-Hami are not part of the swing.]

region.text: the Four Garrisons of Anxi in the Tarim Basin

ledger.note: 670: the fight for the Four Garrisons begins. 'In 670 the Tibetan Empire routed a Tang army at the Battle of Dafei River and attacked Gumo as well as captured Qiuci'; the protectorate's seat moved to Suyab.

region.text: Qiuci and the Western Regions

ledger.note: 673: the Tang retake Qiuci. 'The Tang also captured Qiuci and established control over the Western Regions in the same year.' region.text: Lesser Bolü, the Gilgit valley

region.text: the Anxi and Beiting protectorates

ledger.note: 763: the second fight for the Tarim begins: Yanqi 763, Qiuci 787, the garrisons 790, Yutian 792, with Anxi and Beiting cut off from the Tang after 764.

region.text: Chang'an, the Tang capital

ledger.note: 763 October: the Tibetans occupy Chang'an. 'Tibet occupied Chang'an with an army of 200 thousand soldiers' (Tang-Tibet relations page, October); the Tibetan Empire page: 'late 763'.

region.text: Chang'an

ledger.note: 763: the Tibetans leave Chang'an after 'fifteen days' (Tibetan Empire page). The Tang-Tibet relations page says they withdrew after 15 days; the end month is inferred from the October start.

region.text: Liang Prefecture, the Hexi Corridor and the Longyou land west of Long Mountain; Shazhou (Dunhuang) and Guazhou excepted, they come with the 786 gain

ledger.note: 764: the Hexi Corridor falls. 'In 764 the Tibetan Empire invaded the Hexi Corridor and conquered Liang Prefecture, cutting off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates from the Tang dynasty'; a footnote has the Hexi Army Defense Command falling to the Tibetans in 760. Region: the Hexi and Gansu land Cliopatria's 768 shape adds to the 751 shape. [Author fix ea-04-b, 2026-10-19, after the review: a 200 km disc around Dunhuang is taken out of this gain. The Guiyi Circuit page has the Tibetans occupy Shazhou 'around the 770s or the 780s', dates 'the beginning of Tibetan rule over Dunhuang' to 786 and gives no date for Guazhou, so Shazhou and Guazhou belong to the 786 event (/ledger/34), not to 764. The page dates none of the Hexi cities between Liangzhou (764) and Shazhou (786), so the rest of the corridor stays here at confidence 2.]

region.text: Hexi and Longyou, 'cutting off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates'

ledger.note: 764: the fight for Hexi and Longyou begins and runs to the 783 treaty.

region.text: the Tang-Tibetan frontier, 'near Long Mountain' (Tang-Tibet relations page)

ledger.note: 783: a treaty fixes the border. 'A 783 treaty between the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty defined the borders' (an attempt at a peace treaty followed in 787, and a Sino-Tibetan treaty was agreed in 821/822 under Ralpachen).

region.text: Shazhou (Dunhuang) and Guazhou

ledger.note: 786: Shazhou (Dunhuang) falls. The Guiyi Circuit page has Shazhou under Tibetan occupation from 'the 770s or 780s' and 'another passage dates the start of Tibetan rule to 786'. [Author fix ea-04-b, 2026-10-19, after the review: since the 764 gain (/ledger/31) and the 768-783 corrections now leave out a 200 km disc around Dunhuang, this is the event that brings Shazhou and Guazhou to Tibet. The Guiyi Circuit page: 'From the beginning of Tibetan rule over Dunhuang (786)' and, for the end, 'In 848, Zhang Yichao, a resident of Shazhou, led an uprising and captured Shazhou and Guazhou from the Tibetans'; it gives no date for the Tibetan capture of Guazhou.]

region.text: Qiuci (Kucha), the seat of the Anxi protectorate

ledger.note: 787: Qiuci falls to Tibet for the last time. 'In 787 the Tibetan Empire conquered Qiuci.'

region.text: the remaining garrisons of the Tarim (Shule, Gumo, Shache)

ledger.note: 790: the last Anxi garrisons fall. 'Most sources agree that the last vestiges of the protectorate and its garrisons were defeated by Tibetan forces by 790.' [Reviewer ea-04-b: confidence 3 -> 2; the page dates the end only 'by 790' and does not say what happened to Shule, Shache or Gumo.]

region.text: Beiting (Tingzhou, Beshbalik)

ledger.note: 790: Beiting is occupied. 'Tibet occupied the four Anxi towns and Beiting' (Tang-Tibet relations page); the Uyghur page has the Uyghurs and Tang 'defeated by Tibetan Empire at Tingzhou (Beshbalik)' in 790.

region.text: Tingzhou (Beshbalik), Beiting and the Turfan basin

ledger.note: 790: the Uyghurs fight the Tibetans for Beiting and Turfan, a war that runs to 823.

region.text: Yutian (Khotan)

ledger.note: 792: Khotan falls. 'In 792 the Tibetan Empire conquered Yutian'; the page adds 'It is unclear what happened to Shule (Kashgar), Shache (Yarkand), or Gumo (Aksu)'.

region.text: the Anxi and Beiting protectorates

ledger.note: 792: the second Tarim contest ends with the whole Tarim in Tibetan hands.

region.text: Beiting (Dzungaria) and Gaochang (the Turfan basin)

ledger.note: 792: the Uyghurs take Gaochang and Beiting. 'In 792, the Uyghurs, led by Qutluq's son Baoyi Qaghan, defeated the Tibetans and Karluks, taking Gaochang'; in 791 'the Tibetans and Karluks suffered another defeat against the Uyghurs at Beiting'.

region.text: Nanzhao, the client and ally of the Tibetan Empire

ledger.note: 794: Nanzhao breaks with Tibet. Yimouxun 'launched the battle of Shenchuan to break up with Tibet and switched sides to the Tang' (the Tianbao War page blames Tibet's heavy taxes and military service).

region.text: Beiting and the Turfan basin (and Liang Province, per the page)

ledger.note: 808: the last dated Uyghur-Tibetan gain. 'The Uyghurs seized Liang Province from the Tibetans'; the Tibetans are back in Hexi by 848 (Guiyi Circuit page), so no permanent loss is drawn and the regain is undated.

region.text: the empire's land at its end, passing to the rival Tibetan lords

ledger.note: 842: Langdarma is assassinated and the empire breaks apart. He 'was assassinated, apparently by a Buddhist hermit, in 842' and 'the Battle of U-Yor that arose over Langdarma's successor led to the collapse of the Tibetan Empire' (no year); infobox 'Disestablished: 842/848'. The Tang-Tibet relations page has other dates (Langdarma shot dead 846).

wars.name: Tibetan attack on Songzhou
wars.outcome: Songtsen Gampo's embassy of 634 asked for a marriage alliance; when it was refused Tibet attacked Tang affiliates in 637 and 638 and the frontier city of Songzhou. No ground held on the pages; Princess Wencheng left China in 640.
wars.note: The Songtsen Gampo page also has a Songzhou campaign 'in 635-36'; the Tang-Tibet relations page has Songtsen Gampo invade the Tuyuhun in 636 over a declined proposal.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of Zhangzhung
wars.outcome: Zhangzhung submitted in 634 (Tang Annals) or was overrun in 645 (Stein); it disappeared as a kingdom.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of the Tuyuhun

zones.text: the Tuyuhun ('Azha) lands around Koko Nor

wars.outcome: 'In 635-36, the Emperor attacked and defeated the Tuyuhun ('Azha)'; the kingdom 'was defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture' in 663 (669 on the Tang-Tibet relations page).

wars.name: Tang-Tibetan war for the Four Garrisons
wars.outcome: Tibet won at Dafei River in 670 and held the Tarim; the Tang retook Qiuci in 673, lost it in 677, won in 679 under Pei Xingjian, withdrew in 686, lost the region in 687 and recovered it under Wang Xiaojie in 692.
wars.note: In 690 the Tibetans defeated a Tang army at Issyk-Kul.

wars.name: Tibetan campaigns in Gilgit and Baltistan

zones.text: Lesser Bolü (Gilgit), Greater Bolü (Baltistan) and Wakhan

wars.outcome: Attacks on Lesser Bolü in 656 and on Wakhan; Tibetan conquests of Gilgit in 710 and 737, a Tang restoration in 722 and Gao Xianzhi's capture in 747; in 754 'Tang forces defeated Baltistan (Greater Bolü) and Tibetan forces'.

wars.name: Tibetan-Tang fighting over Aksu and the Stone City
wars.outcome: Tibetan attacks on the Stone City in 694, 717, 720 (seized), 741 (sacked); Tang defeat there in 745; Tang recovery in 749. Aksu attacked in 717 by a Turgesh, Arab and Tibetan force.

wars.name: Tianbao War

zones.text: Yunnan, where Nanzhao took 32 native counties in 750

wars.outcome: Nanzhao captured 32 native counties in 750, turned to Tibet when the Tang refused peace, and with the Tibetans destroyed Li Mi's 70,000 in 754; the Tang could not attack Nanzhao again.

wars.name: Tibetan capture of Chang'an
wars.outcome: The Tibetans reached Chang'an in late 763 and occupied it for fifteen days.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of Hexi and Anxi

zones.text: Liang Prefecture, then the corridor to Shazhou
Yanqi 763, Qiuci 787, the garrisons by 790, Yutian 792

wars.outcome: Liang Prefecture fell in 764, cutting off Anxi and Beiting; Shazhou in 786; the last Anxi garrisons by 790 and Yutian in 792. A 783 treaty 'defined the borders' and a 787 peace attempt failed.

wars.name: Uyghur-Tibetan war

zones.text: Beiting, Tingzhou and the Turfan basin

wars.outcome: The Tibetans beat the Uyghurs and Tang at Tingzhou in 790 but the Uyghurs won at Beiting in 791 and took Gaochang in 792; they seized Liang Province in 808, a Tibetan raid reached within two days of Ordu-Baliq in 816, a Tibetan force was repulsed in 821 and war went on in 823.

wars.name: Battle of Shenchuan
wars.outcome: Nanzhao broke with Tibet and switched to the Tang; in 795 Yimouxun attacked a Tibetan stronghold in 'Kunming' and in 801 the Tibetan force was beaten at Dulu.

wars.name: Tibetan civil war after Langdarma
wars.outcome: After Langdarma's death 'the two princes Yumtan and Osung ... fought for the throne and initiated a civil war'; the Battle of U-Yor led to the collapse of the empire. 'Between 842 and 1247, no central authority was in control of Tibet.'

certainty.note: The plateau, the Tarim, Gilgit and the Yunnan marches were approximate lines; the Tang frontier by Long Mountain and the Chiling boundary monument (731, Tang-Tibet relations page) were agreed lines but their courses are not on the pages.
The Tang-Tibetan frontier is sharp from the 783 treaty that 'defined the borders' and the 821/822 treaty, but no page gives its course; the Uyghur, Tarim and Yunnan frontiers stay soft.

notes:
Written 2026-10-19 by the ea-04-b research agent from twelve opened pages (see sources; nine for the empire proper: Tibetan Empire, Protectorate General to Pacify the West, Songtsen Gampo, Sino-Tibetan relations during the Tang dynasty, Tang-Tibet Treaty Inscription, Guiyi Circuit, Uyghur Khaganate, List of emperors of Tibet, Ladakh; plus Nanzhao, Tianbao War and Era of Fragmentation, opened for the nanzhao and tibetans dossiers). Three guessed URLs for the 821/822 treaty article (Sino-Tibetan_Treaty_of_821%E2%80%93822, Sino-Tibetan_treaty_of_821/822, Sino-Tibetan_Treaty_of_821) returned URL_NOT_FOUND; the Tang-Tibet Treaty Inscription page replaced it and is thin (no border course). The Seshat page (cn_tibet_k) was not opened.

Cliopatria row: 'Tibetan Empire' 623..849, 25 shapes. The dossier ends the state in 842 (Langdarma's assassination; infobox 'Disestablished: 842/848') and gives the empire's 842-849 shape to the new state tibetans (its tibetans_842 keyframe), so that Cliopatria's row 'Tibetans' (850..1259) continues it. Shapes that need correcting: 674 and 682 hold the whole Tarim, Dzungaria and Turfan though the pages have the Four Garrisons swinging (670, 673, 677, 679, 686/687, 692); 757 (wrong) to 783 hold the whole Tarim and Hexi from 757 though the pages date Yanqi 763, Liang 764, Shazhou 786 (770s/780s on the page), Qiuci 787, the garrisons 790, Yutian 792; 763-767 reaches Chang'an for five years though the Tibetans stayed fifteen days; 793-840 hold Dzungaria and the Turfan basin though the Uyghurs took Beiting and Gaochang in 791-792. Infobox area 4.6 M km2 (c. 800) against Cliopatria 3.86 M km2 (ratio 0.84) and the corrected 3.59 M km2 (0.78).

Disagreements between pages, resolved as stated in the events: Tuyuhun's fall 663 (Tibetan Empire), 669 (Tang-Tibet relations), 670 (the Tuyuhun infobox, per the ea-04-a notes); Khotan defeated 665-670 (Tibetan Empire) or conquered 792 (Protectorate page); Zhangzhung 634 (Tang Annals, Ladakh) or 645 (Stein, Songtsen Gampo page); the fall of the Hexi Army Defense Command 760 (a footnote on the Protectorate page) or Liang Prefecture 764; Shazhou 'the 770s or 780s' or 786 (Guiyi Circuit page); Nanzhao under Tibet from 750 (Tibetan Empire) or allied from 754 (Nanzhao page); Chang'an occupied in October 763 (Tang-Tibet relations page) or 18 November 763 (the ea-04-a Tang dossier, from the An Lushan page); Langdarma killed in 842 (Tibetan Empire) or 846 (Tang-Tibet relations), Trisong Detsen's death 841 there against 797 in the list; Trisong Detsen's reign 753 (infobox) or 755 (list). The ruler list page prints overlapping spans (Songtsen Gampo 614-648 and 655-660 around Gungsong Gungtsen 649-655).

Not modelled, page silent or no shape effect: Nepal (the Tibetans restored the Licchavi king in 641; ally, not territory); the Kashmir mirror events (the kashmir dossier has a 656 loss, a 661 contest and 747/748 events against this state; the Ladakh page says only that 'Baltistan and Ladakh were at the centre of these struggles' of the Tang and Tibet, with no Kashmir dates); Greater Bolü (Baltistan) as a client (754 battle only); the Nanzhao raids on Tibetan strongholds (795, 801); the Tarim between 792 and 842 (no page gives a loss; Khotan's independence in 851 is in the kingdom-of-khotan dossier); the Chiling boundary monument of 731 (no course); the 703 Jang invasion's extent. Cliopatria's 692-719 shapes already hold the Stone City which the Protectorate page gives to the Tang until 720.

Counterparts without a dossier: Sumpa, Zhangzhung (a kingdom, 634/645), Lesser Bolü / Gilgit, White and Black Mywa peoples, Guiyi Circuit (848-1036; suggested guiyi-circuit, named in the ea-04-a notes). Family: no Tibetan family exists in colours.json; 'india' is the nearest (its hue band 280-340 holds the assigned tibet/tibetans colours); a 'tibet' family would be better.

Gazetteer names wanted: the region 'Zhangzhung' (Ngari, western Tibet); places 'Charklik' (Ruoqiang, the Stone City, here approximated by a 300 km disc around Qiemo), 'Songzhou' (Songpan), 'Wakhan'.

Author revision after the review (ea-04-b, 2026-10-19): (1) Shazhou and Guazhou (Dunhuang) are no longer Tibetan from 764. The reviewer found all 42 cells of a 60 km Dunhuang disc inside the 764 gain and inside the 768, 772 and 783 corrections, which made the 786 gain (/ledger/34) a no-op and drew the west end of the corridor Tibetan 22 years before the Guiyi Circuit page dates it ('Around the 770s or the 780s ... occupied by the Tibetans'; 'the beginning of Tibetan rule over Dunhuang (786)'; re-read 2026-10-19). A 200 km disc around Dunhuang is now subtracted from /ledger/31 and from the corrections of keyframes 768, 772 and 783 (334 cells, about 84,000 km2), and /ledger/34 brings it in 786. The cities between Liangzhou (764) and Shazhou (786) stay undated on the pages: Ganzhou, Suzhou and Yizhou appear only as taken by Zhang Yichao 'by 850'. (2) The reviewer's four applied fixes were checked on the file: the Tarim-only region of the 670, 673, 679, 687 and 692 swings, the Yutian counterpart of the 666 gain, the tuyuhun counterpart of the 638 step and confidence 2 for the 790 gain. The counterpart name 'Yutian (Kingdom of Khotan)' has no dossier (the Kingdom of Khotan dossier begins in 851). (3) Not mine, routed to ea-04-a (tang-dynasty): the 717-749 Aksu/Stone City contest, the 747 Gilgit loss, the 749 Stone City loss, the 757 Gilgit gain, the 763 Yanqi gain and the 786 Dunhuang gain have no mirror there; the Tang ledger has only the 787 Kuqa loss in 785-787 and only the Chang'an occupation in 762-763. The Protectorate page sentences are quoted in the events. Disagreement with the reviewer: none on the Dunhuang finding; the Dunhuang disc is 200 km as asked (it also takes the eastern approaches around Guazhou, about 120 km away, which is intended).
